title: Hard drive: neodymium magnets, platters and spindle motor
summary: Every spinning hard drive holds one or two powerful neodymium magnets on steel plates, mirror-polished platters and a small brushless spindle motor. You need small Torx drivers. The magnets snap together hard and the glass platters in many drives shatter.

steps.text: Take the drive out of the computer or enclosure. Solid-state drives (no moving parts, often very light) have no magnets: skip them.

Remove every screw on the lid. Most drives use small Torx screws (T6–T9). Look for a hidden screw under the label: press around the label and over any "warranty" sticker with a fingernail to find the hole.
Pry the lid off from a corner with a flat blade. It may also be held by a foil seal around the edge: cut it with a knife.
Find the voice-coil magnet in the corner by the arm. Undo its 1–2 screws and lever the top magnet plate up with a flat screwdriver.
steps.warn: The magnet grabs anything steel. Keep fingers off the gap, keep magnets away from pacemakers, and slide them apart, don't pull.

steps.text: Undo the pivot screw of the arm and swing the arm off the platters. Lift out the lower magnet plate the same way as the top.
Undo the small screws in the ring clamp on the spindle hub, lift the clamp, then lift off each platter and its spacer.
steps.warn: Many laptop and some desktop platters are glass. They shatter into sharp splinters if dropped or bent. Hold them by the edges.

steps.text: Leave the magnet on its steel plate unless you need it bare. To free it, clamp the plate and bend it slowly; the magnet pops off.
steps.warn: Wear eye protection. Neodymium magnets are brittle and chip or shatter if they snap together.

steps.text: The spindle motor is pressed into the base casting. Keep the whole base, or drive the motor out with a punch from the underside.
Store magnets in pairs, stuck together through a spacer of wood or card, away from electronics.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Voice-coil magnets.** Curved neodymium magnets, one or two per drive, bonded to steel plates. The plates focus the field: a plate magnet holds tools to a bench, picks nails and filings out of dirt, or makes a strong door catch. Bare magnets go into small generators and magnetometers.
- **Platters.** Aluminium or glass discs with a mirror finish. A platter is an excellent signal mirror: aim the flash through the centre hole at your target. Also small reflectors.
- **Spindle motor.** A small 3-phase brushless motor. Run it from a brushless motor driver, or spin it to make a little 3-phase AC (needs a rectifier).
- **Arm bearing.** A tiny precision bearing pair.
- **Screws.** Small Torx screws for small projects.

## Variations

- Desktop drives (3.5 inch) usually have two big magnet plates and aluminium platters. Laptop drives (2.5 inch) have smaller magnets and glass platters more often.
- Some drives use a single magnet with a plain steel top plate.
- Helium-filled drives have the lid welded on; cut around the edge with a grinder or skip them.

## Magnet safety

- Two drive magnets can crush skin between them. Keep them apart with spacers.
- Keep them away from watches, cards, phones, compasses and medical implants.
- Don't heat them: neodymium magnets lose strength above about 80 °C.

## What to leave

- The circuit board on the underside holds the motor driver chip and little else of use.
- The small filter pads inside.
